title: Do other animals feel? Bee dances, elephant rumbles and the question of consciousness

summary.text: A hermit crab in a good shell puts up with a small electric shock, but one in a poor shell climbs out. What does that tell us about what the crab feels? In this lesson you will read a bee's dance, test a prize against an ice cube on yourself, and watch one animal.
summary.art: A hermit crab half out of a small plain shell on wet sand, looking towards a larger, better shell, with a child crouching nearby holding an ice cube over a bowl.

intro.hook: Someone taps just below your kneecap and your leg kicks. Someone offers you the last piece of mysore pak and you stop to think about your sister. Both are things your body did. What is the difference between them?
intro.text: The kick happens the same way every time, whatever else is going on. The sweet is different. You weigh how much you want it against how your sister will feel. Scientists use this difference to study other animals. They cannot ask a bee or a crab how they feel. But they can watch whether the animal weighs one thing against another. In this lesson you will run that test on yourself. You will also learn two ways animals send detailed messages: the dance of the honeybee and the low rumble of the elephant.
intro.art: A child at a table with one piece of mysore pak on a plate between her and her younger sister, both looking at it.

outcomes: I can explain how a honeybee's waggle dance gives the direction and distance of food, and how scientists checked that other bees use it.
I can describe how elephants keep in touch with rumbles too low for us to hear, through the air and through the ground.
I can tell an emotion, which can be measured from outside, from a feeling, which is what the emotion is like from inside.
I can run a fair trade-off test, and explain what it shows that watching a reflex does not show.
I can name four kinds of evidence scientists look for when they ask whether an animal feels pain or pleasure.
I can explain the main views in the debate about animal consciousness, and what evidence each view asks for.
I can write what an animal did separately from my guess about what they felt.
I can explain why the answer to 'who feels?' changes laws and the way people treat other animals.

terms.meaning: A sound, movement, smell or touch that one animal makes and that changes what another animal does.
terms.example: A crow's loud call makes other crows look up.
terms.art: A crow calling on a wire while two other crows turn their heads towards her.

terms.meaning: A dance a honeybee does on the comb after she finds food. The direction of her run and how long she waggles tell other bees where to fly.
terms.example: A bee runs straight up the comb, waggling for two seconds.
terms.art: A honeybee on a comb with a wavy line drawn behind her and other bees touching her with their antennae.

terms.meaning: Something that stands for something else by a rule. The symbol does not look like the thing it stands for.
terms.example: 'Up' on the comb stands for 'towards the sun'.
terms.art: An arrow pointing up on a honeycomb, joined by a dotted line to a small sun over a field.

terms.meaning: Sound that is too low in pitch for human ears. People hear down to about 20 vibrations each second, and infrasound is lower than that.
terms.example: Part of an elephant's rumble is infrasound.
terms.art: An elephant with wide wavy lines spreading out from her forehead, and a child nearby cupping an ear and hearing nothing.

terms.meaning: A long, very low call that elephants make. We hear only the higher part of it, as a soft growl.
terms.example: A mother elephant rumbles and her calf walks back to her.
terms.art: A mother elephant with her mouth slightly open and a calf turning towards her.

terms.meaning: A message that travels as a tiny shaking of the ground.
terms.example: An elephant's rumble also shakes the soil a little, and that shaking spreads outwards.
terms.art: A cross-section of ground with small ripples travelling from one elephant's feet to another's.

terms.meaning: A state of the whole body and brain that gets an animal ready to act, such as fear or joy. It can be measured from outside: the heart, the muscles, the chemicals in the blood and what the animal does.
terms.example: A frightened deer has a fast heart and tight muscles, and runs.
terms.art: A spotted deer with ears up and a small drawing of a fast heartbeat line beside her.

terms.meaning: What an emotion or a sensation is like from the inside, for the one who has it.
terms.example: Only you know what your fear feels like.
terms.art: A child with a hand on her chest and her eyes closed.

terms.meaning: Being able to feel things as good or bad, such as pain, comfort, hunger or pleasure.
terms.example: A law in Britain names crabs and octopuses as sentient animals.
terms.art: A crab, an octopus, a hen and a child drawn side by side in a row.

terms.meaning: Having any experience at all. If there is something it is like to be you, you are conscious. Scientists and thinkers do not agree on one full definition.
terms.example: There is something it is like to taste rasam.
terms.art: A child tasting rasam from a steel tumbler with a look of concentration.

terms.meaning: A fast reaction of the body that happens the same way each time, before any weighing of what else matters.
terms.example: You blink when a puff of air hits your eye.
terms.art: An eye blinking as a small puff of air from a straw reaches it.

terms.meaning: The body detecting damage, or something that could cause damage. Special nerve endings called nociceptors do this job.
terms.example: Nerve endings in your finger fire when you touch a thorn.
terms.art: A fingertip touching a thorn with a small signal travelling up a nerve.

terms.meaning: Giving up some of one thing that matters to get more of another.
terms.example: You stand in the hot sun a little longer to finish the cricket over.
terms.art: A child batting in bright sun with a shady tree in the background.

terms.meaning: A test of mood. The animal learns that one signal means something good and another means something bad. Then scientists give an in-between signal and see which way the animal takes it.
terms.example: Bees who had just been shaken treated an in-between smell as bad.
terms.art: A honeybee facing three small dishes, one marked sweet, one marked bitter and one in the middle with a question mark.

terms.meaning: A chemical that one cell releases to pass a message to other cells. Serotonin and dopamine are two of them.
terms.example: Dopamine is released in a brain when something turns out better than expected.
terms.art: Two nerve cells with small dots crossing the gap between them.

terms.meaning: A test that lets an animal choose between two things, to find out which one they want and how much.
terms.example: Hens offered a wire floor or a floor of loose litter chose the litter.
terms.art: A hen standing at a fork between a wire-floored pen and a pen with loose earth.

terms.meaning: Giving another animal human thoughts and feelings that the evidence does not show.
terms.example: Saying a gecko on the wall 'is bored of us'.
terms.art: A gecko on a wall with a thought bubble showing a television, crossed out.

explanations.concept: An emotion and a feeling are two different things
explanations.description: When a street dog hears a cracker burst, her heart speeds up and her muscles tighten. She tucks her tail and runs. All of that can be measured. Scientists call it an emotion, here the emotion of fear. What the fear is like for the dog is a different matter. That inside part is called a feeling, and no instrument measures it. This is true for people too. A doctor can count your pulse, but she cannot feel your fear. So scientists study emotions directly. They work out feelings from evidence, in other animals and in other people. Animals feel. The hard part is showing it in a way that convinces someone who doubts it.
examples: A dog's fast heart after a cracker bursts is part of the emotion. What that moment is like for her is the feeling.
A friend says 'my stomach hurts'. You believe her, though you have never felt her stomach.
A hen's body temperature changes when she is handled. That is a measurement, not yet a feeling.
explanations.art: A street dog running with her tail tucked while a cracker bursts behind her, with a small heartbeat line drawn above her.
explanations.definition: An emotion is a state of the body and brain that prepares an animal to act, and it can be measured from outside. A feeling is what that state is like from inside.

explanations.concept: The waggle dance: a message that stands for a place
explanations.description: A honeybee who has found good flowers comes home and dances on the comb, usually in the dark. She runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and runs again. The direction of the run is a code. Straight up the comb means 'fly towards the sun'. A run 60 degrees to the right of straight up means 'fly 60 degrees to the right of the sun'. The longer she waggles, the farther the food. Why does this count as more than a reaction? Because the dance is about a place that is far away and out of sight. 'Up' does not look like the sun. It stands for the sun by a rule that all the bees share. Karl von Frisch worked the code out in the 1940s. The other bees follow the dancer closely and touch her with their antennae, their feelers, because they cannot see her in the dark.
examples: A run straight down the comb means the food lies directly away from the sun.
A bee who waggles for one second sends her sisters a shorter way than a bee who waggles for three.
The sun moves across the sky, so a bee who dances for a long time slowly changes her angle to match.
explanations.art: A honeybee on a vertical comb running upwards at a slant with a wavy trail, an arrow marked 'up', and above the hive a sun and a patch of flowers set at the same slant.
explanations.definition: The waggle dance is a honeybee's signal for where food is. The angle of the waggle run from straight up gives the direction from the sun. The length of the waggle gives the distance.

explanations.description: How does the dancer know how far she flew? In 2000, Mandyam Srinivasan, a scientist born in Bengaluru, and his team tested this. They made bees fly to sugar through a narrow tunnel only a few metres long. The walls had a busy pattern. When the bees came home, they danced as if they had flown hundreds of metres. In the narrow tunnel, the pattern rushed past the bees' eyes very fast. So a bee measures distance by how much scenery streams past her eyes as she flies. She does not measure the energy she used or the time she took. This also shows that the dance reports what the bee experienced on her flight. It is her measurement, with the errors her way of measuring brings.
examples: From a moving auto, nearby shops rush past and far hills hardly move.
Bees who flew a few metres through a narrow patterned tunnel danced for a far place.
A bee flying over a plain lake sees little streaming past and may dance for too short a distance.
explanations.art: A honeybee flying through a narrow tunnel with a black and white pattern on the walls, and streak lines showing the pattern rushing past her eyes.
explanations.definition: A flying honeybee measures distance by optic flow, which is how much the scene moves across her eyes during the flight.

explanations.concept: Do the other bees really use the dance?
explanations.description: For years, some scientists doubted the dance. Adrian Wenner and Patrick Wells showed in the 1960s that bees can find food by smell alone. They said the dance might not be needed at all. That was a fair challenge. In 1975, James Gould made dancers point to a place they had never visited, and the followers flew to that place. In 2005, Joe Riley's team stuck tiny radar aerials on bees who had followed a dance. Then they carried those bees to a new starting spot. The bees flew the direction and distance of the dance from the new spot, and so arrived at the wrong place. Smell could not explain that. Today most scientists accept that the dance sends bees to the right area, and that smell and sight then find the flowers. Whether to call the dance a language is still argued over.
examples: Followers moved to a new starting spot still flew the danced direction and distance.
Near the flowers, a bee uses the smell she picked up from the dancer's body.
A dance has a symbol for direction, but bees do not make new 'sentences' with it.

perspectives.who: Karl von Frisch, James Gould and Joe Riley
perspectives.explanation: The dance carries direction and distance, and other bees use that information. The radar tracks show bees flying the danced course even from the wrong starting place.
Smell is enough for bees to find food. They pushed others to test the dance properly. Most scientists now think they were right that smell matters, and wrong that the dance does not.
The dance uses symbols and is about things that are not present, and both are rare among signals. But it covers only a few subjects and has no grammar, so they do not call it a language.

explanations.art: A honeybee with a thin radar aerial on her back flying over a field, with a dotted straight path drawn from a release point.

explanations.concept: India's honeybees dance in different dialects
explanations.description: India has several kinds of honeybee, and each dances a little differently. The dwarf honeybee builds one small comb in the open, around a twig. She dances on the flat top of the comb and points her run straight at the food. She needs no code for direction. The rock bee builds the huge combs that hang under flyovers, water tanks and tall branches. She dances on the upright comb and uses the 'up means sun' code. The Asian hive bee lives in dark hollows and uses the same code. In 2020, a team working in Bengaluru, which included Patrick Kohl, Neethu Thulasi, Ebi Antony George and Axel Brockmann, timed the dances of all three. For the same distance, the Asian hive bee waggled longer than the rock bee. The Asian hive bee feeds close to home and the rock bee flies far. So each kind of bee has a scale that suits the distances she flies.
examples: A dwarf honeybee's run on the flat comb top points like a finger at the flowers.
One second of waggling means a longer flight for a rock bee than for an Asian hive bee.
A map of a town and a map of India use different scales for the same reason.
explanations.art: Three combs side by side: a small comb around a twig with a bee dancing on the flat top, a huge hanging comb under a ledge, and a comb inside a hollow tree trunk.
explanations.definition: A dance dialect is one kind of bee's own scale for how much waggling stands for how much distance.

explanations.concept: Elephant rumbles: calls too low for us to hear
explanations.description: In 1984, Katy Payne sat beside the Asian elephants at a zoo in Portland, in the United States. She felt a faint throbbing in the air, though she heard nothing. It reminded her of standing near the biggest pipes of a church organ. She came back with recorders that pick up very low sound. When the tapes were played fast, the low calls became high enough to hear. The elephants had been calling all along. A rumble's lowest part is about 14 to 24 vibrations each second, and human ears stop at about 20. Why would an elephant call so low? Low sounds lose less of their energy to the air, and they bend around trees and hills, so they travel much farther than high sounds. A herd spread over a forest can stay in touch. In tests in Africa, elephants answered recorded rumbles played from two kilometres away. At Mudumalai in Tamil Nadu, Smita Nair and her colleagues sorted the calls of wild Asian elephants into four kinds: trumpets, roars, chirps and rumbles.
examples: At a temple festival you feel the big drum in your chest from far away, but the small bells fade quickly.
A mother elephant rumbles and her family, out of sight among the trees, turns towards her.
When an elephant rumbles, the skin on her forehead flutters.
explanations.art: A forest valley with one elephant family in the foreground and a second family far away among trees, joined by long, wide wavy lines.
explanations.definition: A rumble is a long, very low elephant call. Its lowest part is infrasound, which is sound below the lowest pitch people can hear.

explanations.description: A rumble also shakes the ground a little, and that shaking spreads outwards through the soil. Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell tested whether elephants notice it. In Namibia her team played recorded alarm rumbles into the ground only, with nothing in the air. Elephant families at a waterhole bunched closer together and turned to face the source. So elephants can pick up a message through the ground. How do they sense it? An elephant's foot has a thick cushion of fat and many nerve endings that sense pressure, and so does the tip of her trunk. The shaking may also travel up her leg bones to her ears. Scientists are still working out which path matters most, and how much wild elephants depend on ground messages in daily life.
examples: Elephants at a waterhole went still and bunched together when alarm rumbles were played through the soil.
A listening elephant may lean forward and put more weight on her front feet.
You can hear a soft thump better with your ear on the floor than standing up.

perspectives.explanation: Elephants respond to rumbles sent through the ground alone, so they can use the ground as a second channel when the air is noisy or the wind is wrong.
The tests show elephants can detect ground signals. They do not yet show how often wild elephants rely on them, or from how far.

explanations.art: A side view of an elephant standing still with one front foot pressed flat, and ripples in the soil reaching the foot from the left.

explanations.concept: Names, comfort and the dead: what elephants do for each other
explanations.description: In 2024, Michael Pardo and his team studied hundreds of rumbles recorded in Kenya. A computer could often work out which elephant a rumble was meant for. When the team played a rumble back, the elephant it was first meant for answered faster than she answered other rumbles. So elephants may call each other by something like a name. The result is new and needs repeating. In 2014, Joshua Plotnik and Frans de Waal watched Asian elephants in Thailand. When one elephant was upset, others walked over, touched her face with their trunks and chirped. In 2022, Sanjeeta Sharma Pokharel, Nachiketha Sharma and Raman Sukumar gathered videos of Asian elephants around their dead. Some mothers carried a dead calf for days. Elephants feel, and these are the acts we would expect from an animal who cares about others. Scientists agree about what the elephants did. They disagree about what name to give it.
examples: A calf squeals, and an older cousin walks over and puts her trunk in the calf's mouth.
A mother carries her dead calf on her tusks for several days.
An elephant lifts her head and answers one recorded rumble much faster than another.

perspectives.who: Frans de Waal, Joyce Poole and Raman Sukumar's group
perspectives.explanation: Comforting, name-like calls and staying with the dead are best explained by elephants having emotions such as distress and attachment, as we do.
The acts are real and carefully recorded. But 'grief' is a word for a human feeling. We should describe exactly what the elephants do, and keep testing other explanations.
Words like 'grief' and 'anger' are sorted partly by human language and culture. Other animals surely have pleasant and unpleasant states, but those states may not divide up the way our words do.

explanations.art: Two Asian elephants standing close, one touching the other's face with the tip of her trunk.

explanations.concept: How to test for a feeling: the trade-off
explanations.description: A reflex happens the same way whatever else is going on. A feeling can be weighed against other things that matter. That gives scientists something to test. In 2009, Robert Elwood and Mirjam Appel gave hermit crabs a small electric shock inside their shells. Hermit crabs live in empty sea shells and care a great deal which kind they get. Crabs in the kind of shell they like less left it more readily. Crabs in a good shell stayed through the same shock. In 2022, Matilda Gibbons and her team gave bumblebees a choice between a hot feeder and a cool one. When the hot feeder held much sweeter sugar water, more bees put up with the heat. Both animals weighed harm against reward, as you do when you hold on to something uncomfortable for a reason. Weighing does not prove a feeling. It does show that a simple reflex is not the whole explanation.
examples: A hermit crab in a poor shell leaves at a shock that a crab in a good shell sits through.
A bumblebee walks onto a hot feeder only when the sugar there is much sweeter.
You keep holding a hot dosa plate because the table is two steps away.
explanations.art: A hermit crab climbing out of a small plain shell on the left, and another hermit crab staying inside a larger shell on the right, each with a small lightning mark beside the shell.
explanations.definition: A trade-off test changes what an animal can gain, and checks whether that changes how much harm the animal accepts. A reflex does not change with the reward. A weighed choice does.

explanations.concept: Moods in small bodies: the pessimistic bee and the anxious crayfish
explanations.description: A person in a low mood expects the worst from an unclear sign. In 2011, Melissa Bateson, Geraldine Wright and their team tested this in honeybees. The bees learned that one smell meant sugar and another meant a bitter drink. Then half the bees were shaken for a minute, as if an animal were attacking the hive. Shaken bees more often treated in-between smells as the bitter one. The levels of several signalling chemicals in their bodies had dropped too. In 2014, Pascal Fossat's team gave crayfish mild electric shocks. Afterwards the crayfish kept to the dark arms of a tank and avoided the lit ones. A medicine that calms anxious people made them explore the light again. So a bee and a crayfish can be put into a lasting state that works like a mood.
examples: Shaken bees pulled back from a smell that calm bees were willing to try.
Stressed crayfish stayed in the dark, and went back to the light after a calming medicine.
After a bad morning, you may expect an unclear message from a friend to be bad news.

perspectives.explanation: These animals show the same pattern that we use as a sign of mood in rats, dogs and people. The fair conclusion is that they have states like emotions.
The shaking changed how the bees responded. That shows an emotion-like state of the body. It does not show what the state is like for the bee, or whether it is like anything.

explanations.art: Two honeybees each facing a small dish with a question mark, one reaching forward with her tongue and one leaning back.

explanations.concept: The same signalling chemicals in a bee, a crayfish and you
explanations.description: Why did a human medicine calm a crayfish? Because the crayfish's nerves use some of the same signalling chemicals as yours. Serotonin and dopamine carry messages between nerve cells in people, crayfish, bees and worms. People, crayfish and bees share ancestors who lived more than 500 million years ago. Those ancestors already used these chemicals, and their descendants kept them. Some of the chemicals are far older than nerves. Serotonin is also made by plants and fungi. This does not prove that a crayfish's fear feels like yours. The same chemical can do different jobs in different bodies. But it does mean that emotions were not invented by humans. Our emotions run on parts that were in use long before there were any humans.
examples: Dopamine is involved when a bumblebee finds an unexpected drop of sugar, and when you get a surprise treat.
A tomato plant makes serotonin too.
Bees have a chemical called octopamine that does a job like adrenaline in your body.
explanations.art: A simple family tree with a human, a crayfish and a honeybee at the tips, and the same small chemical drawing placed beside each one and at the shared root.
explanations.definition: A signalling chemical is released by one cell to pass a message to another. Many of the signalling chemicals in human brains are also found in insects, crabs, worms and even plants.

explanations.description: Animals feel. A crab, a bee and an elephant each have experiences of their own. Not everyone has thought so. In 1637, Rene Descartes wrote that other animals were like clockwork, moving with nothing felt inside. In 1871, Charles Darwin answered that the minds of humans and other animals differ in amount, not in kind. For much of the 1900s, many scientists refused to talk about animal feelings at all, because feelings cannot be measured. That has changed. In 2012, a group of brain scientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness. In 2024, hundreds of scientists and philosophers signed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. It says the evidence for conscious experience is strong in mammals and birds. It says there is at least a realistic chance of it in all animals with backbones, and in insects, crabs and octopuses. The argument now is about how far it goes and how sure we can be.
examples: A law passed in Britain in 2022 treats crabs, lobsters and octopuses as animals who can feel.
The philosopher Thomas Nagel asked in 1974 what it is like to be a bat, who finds her way by echoes.
You have never felt another person's pain either. You work it out from what they do and say.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin, and the signers of the New York Declaration (2024)
perspectives.explanation: Bodies, brains and behaviour change little by little from one kind of animal to the next. So it would be strange if feeling switched on suddenly in humans. Where the evidence is unsure, we should take the chance of feeling seriously.
The brain circuits that make a rat freeze work without awareness, even in people. A felt emotion may need extra brain parts that only some animals have. Behaviour alone cannot tell us.

perspectives.who: Jain teachers, the scientist J. C. Bose, and philosophers such as Philip Goff
perspectives.explanation: Feeling does not begin with brains. Jain texts count the senses of every living being, down to those with one sense. Bose measured responses in plants and metals. Goff argues that experience is a basic feature of all matter.

explanations.art: A long table with an elephant, a crow, a fish, a crab and a bee sitting on one side and three scientists with notebooks on the other.

explanations.concept: Feeling without a brain like ours
explanations.description: Some people argue that pain needs the wrinkled outer layer of the human brain, called the cortex. Fish, crabs and bees have no such layer. But many animals do the same job with different parts. Birds have no layered cortex, and yet crows plan and solve problems. An octopus has most of her nerve cells in her arms. The insect scientists Andrew Barron and Colin Klein argued in 2016 that the centre of an insect's brain does what the human midbrain does. It puts together the animal's senses, body and needs into one picture to act on. They think that is enough for a simple kind of experience. Under all of this lies a harder puzzle. Nobody can yet explain how the activity of any nerve cells goes with a feeling, even in a human brain. The philosopher David Chalmers named this the 'hard problem' in 1995.
examples: A crow's brain has no layered cortex, but she can make a hook to fish out food.
An octopus's arms do much of their own steering, with little help from her central brain.
A honeybee's brain is about the size of a sesame seed, and she still learns, remembers and decides.

perspectives.explanation: Experience needs a brain centre that joins the animal's senses and needs into one picture. Insects have one, so insects probably have simple experiences.
Pain as we feel it depends on the layered cortex. Fish have none, so we should not assume that fish feel pain.
Even a full map of a brain's activity does not explain why that activity is felt. Until that is solved, no brain test can settle who is conscious.

explanations.art: A row of four brains drawn to very different sizes and shapes, labelled human, crow, octopus and honeybee.

explanations.concept: Why it matters: asking animals what they want
explanations.description: If other animals feel, then how we keep them matters to them. In the 1970s, Marian Stamp Dawkins found a way to ask. She let hens choose between a cage and a run with grass, and between a wire floor and loose litter to scratch in. Then she made the choice cost something, to see how much each thing mattered to the hens. Tests like hers are now used to design farms, zoos and laboratories. Vets give fish painkillers after an operation. In 2021, a team led by Jonathan Birch reviewed more than 300 studies for the British government. The law passed the next year treats crabs, lobsters and octopuses as animals who can feel. Many people also argue for a simple rule of caution. When we are unsure whether an animal feels, we should act as if they do.
examples: A zoo hides food in a log so that a bear has something to work out.
Hens given the choice walk to the pen with loose litter.
A fish gets a painkiller in her tank water after an operation.
explanations.art: A hen standing at a small gate between a bare wire pen and a pen with loose earth and grass, with a woman watching from behind a low screen.
explanations.definition: A preference test lets an animal choose between two things, and sometimes pay a cost for one of them. It shows what the animal wants and how much.

agreed.text: Honeybees who follow a waggle dance use the direction and distance it gives.
agreed.evidence: Joe Riley's team tracked followers by radar in 2005. Bees released from a new spot flew the danced course from there and missed the food, so they were not following smell.

agreed.text: Elephants make calls that are partly too low for human ears, and other elephants answer them from far away.
agreed.evidence: Katy Payne's team recorded the calls in 1984. Later, elephants in Africa turned and walked towards recorded rumbles played from two kilometres away.

agreed.text: Emotions, the measurable states of body and brain, are shared widely among animals.
agreed.evidence: Mammals, birds and fish release similar stress chemicals when frightened. Bees and crayfish change how they treat unclear signals after a bad experience.

agreed.text: Crabs, bees and fish do more than react to harm. They guard a hurt place, learn to avoid what hurt them, and weigh harm against reward.
agreed.evidence: Hermit crabs give up poor shells sooner than good ones at the same shock. Bumblebees accept heat for sweeter sugar. Hurt trout stop feeding for a while and rub the sore place.

agreed.text: Nobody can measure a feeling directly, in another animal or in another person.
agreed.evidence: Every instrument measures something outside the feeling: a pulse, a chemical, a brain signal or an act. The feeling is worked out from these.

agreed.text: The evidence for conscious experience is strong for mammals and birds.
agreed.evidence: Hundreds of scientists and philosophers signed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness in 2024, after decades of tests on brains and behaviour.

challenging.claim: Other animals are like clockwork. They move, but nothing is felt inside.
challenging.who: Rene Descartes, a French thinker, in 1637.
challenging.for: Many acts of the body, such as a blink, do run without any weighing. Machines can be built that react to the world.
challenging.against: Animals learn, weigh harm against reward and comfort each other. They share our nerves and signalling chemicals. A clock does none of this.
challenging.context: This view shaped how animals were treated for about three hundred years.

challenging.claim: Fish feel no pain, because they have no cortex.
challenging.who: James Rose in 2002 and Brian Key in 2016.
challenging.for: In people, the cortex is active when pain is felt. Fish have no layered cortex.
challenging.against: Lynne Sneddon found nerve endings for injury in trout in 2003. Hurt trout stopped feeding and rubbed their lips, and a painkiller reduced this. Birds also lack a layered cortex.
challenging.context: This is a claim about which brain parts a feeling needs.

challenging.who: Lars Chittka, in his book The Mind of a Bee (2022), and others.
challenging.for: Bees show mood-like changes, accept heat for a better reward and tend a hurt antenna. Bumblebees roll balls with no reward.
challenging.against: A bee has about a million nerve cells and a very different brain. Some scientists say these results show flexible behaviour, and that this is not yet evidence of experience.
challenging.context: Twenty years ago, few scientists would have asked this question at all.

challenging.claim: Saying that an elephant grieves is anthropomorphism.
challenging.for: Grief is a human word. We could be reading our own feelings into an animal whose experience we have not measured.
challenging.against: Frans de Waal called the opposite mistake anthropodenial: refusing to see a likeness that the evidence supports. Elephants and people are both mammals with similar brain parts for emotion.
challenging.context: Both mistakes are possible, so the wording of each claim has to match the evidence.

challenging.claim: The bee dance is not needed. Bees find food by smell.
challenging.who: Adrian Wenner and Patrick Wells, from the 1960s.
challenging.for: Bees can be led to food by smell alone, and near the flowers they do use smell.
challenging.against: Radar tracks from 2005 show bees flying the danced direction and distance, even when it takes them to the wrong place.
challenging.context: The challenge was useful, because it forced better tests of the dance.

challenging.claim: The more an animal looks like us, the more that animal feels.
challenging.who: A common idea, though few people say it aloud.
challenging.for: Animals close to us on the family tree, such as apes, share the most brain parts with us.
challenging.against: Octopuses and bees are very unlike us, and still pass several tests for emotion-like states. Looking like us is not evidence either way.
challenging.context: This idea decides which animals most laws protect.

big_questions.q: You let go of the ice when it hurt enough. Was that a choice or a reaction? Where is the line between the two?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether the prize changed the moment you let go, and what that tells you.

big_questions.q: A bee's dance stands for a place she cannot see from the hive. Is that a word? What makes something a word?
big_questions.hint: Think about what 'up' means on the comb, and whether the bees could have agreed on a different rule.

big_questions.q: You have never felt a friend's pain. Why are you sure she feels it? Does the same reason work for an elephant, a fish and a bee?
big_questions.hint: List your reasons for believing your friend. Then check each one against each animal.

big_questions.q: A crab weighs a shock against a good shell. Is the weighing the feeling, or only a sign of it?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether a machine could be built to weigh two numbers, and whether that would settle it.

big_questions.q: If we are not sure whether a crab feels pain, how should people treat crabs while we are unsure?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is lost if we are careful and wrong, and what is lost if we are careless and wrong.

big_questions.q: Elephants send rumbles that human ears miss. What other messages might be passing around you right now?
big_questions.hint: Think of smells, very high sounds, the shaking of the ground, and light that our eyes do not pick up.

big_questions.q: Serotonin is in you, in a crayfish and in a tomato plant. What does sharing a chemical tell us, and what does it leave open?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether the same tool can be used for different jobs.

story.title: The Tumbler That Shivered
story.note: A made-up story. Selvi, her mother Rani, Kannagi and Mr Joseph are imagined. Valparai in the Anamalai hills of Tamil Nadu is real. So are the phone messages that warn tea estate workers there when elephants are near, which the Nature Conservation Foundation began. Elephant calves do fall into trenches and tanks, and forest staff free them by breaking one side into a slope. Elephants do call in rumbles too low for people to hear, and Katy Payne first noticed them as a throbbing in the air. The water shivering in a tumbler is imagined.
text: The message reached Amma's phone at half past five. 'Elephants near field number seven. Please stay indoors.' In the workers' lines above Valparai, everyone got the same message, and everyone knew what to do. You brought the washing in. You called the children. You waited, and in ten minutes the herd would cross the road and go down to the stream.
That evening they did not cross.

Selvi ate her dinner at the window, because the window was the best seat in the house. Below her the road bent round the tea bushes. On the bend stood the elephants, dark and close together. Their trunks hung still. An hour went by, and they had not moved the length of a lorry.

People began to grumble from their doorways. The night shift at the factory started at eight. The ration van was stuck on the far side. Mr Joseph, the field supervisor, walked up and down with his torch. 'They are being stubborn,' he said. 'If they are not gone by seven, I will light crackers.'
'You will not,' said Amma. 'You know what the forest people say about crackers.'
Selvi put her steel tumbler on the window sill and reached for more rice. That was when she saw the water.

The top of the water shivered. Tiny rings ran from the edge to the middle and were gone. She looked for a lorry on the road. There was none. Nobody was walking in the room. She held her breath and listened. She heard crickets, a pressure cooker next door, and nothing else.
The water shivered again.

This time she felt something as well. It was very faint, low in her chest, like a flutter. She knew that feeling. At the temple festival last year she had stood beside the big drum. Before she heard each beat, she felt it under her ribs.

Selvi looked at the elephants. The biggest one, an old female, stood at the front. The skin of her forehead was trembling. When it trembled, the water in the tumbler shivered. Then the forehead went still and the water went still. All the elephants spread their ears wide and did not move at all. One of them rested the tip of her trunk on the ground.
'They are doing something,' Selvi said. Nobody heard her.
She watched it happen four more times. The forehead trembled and the water shivered. Then came the stillness, with the ears held wide. She thought it was like someone calling down a well and waiting.
People who are calling are calling to somebody, Selvi thought.

She counted the herd. There were six. She took Amma's phone from the shelf and scrolled back to yesterday's message. 'Herd of seven with one calf, near the check dam.' She counted again. There were six elephants, and none of them was small.
Then she noticed which way they were facing. It was not towards the houses or the road. Every head pointed downhill, past the last row of tea, towards the old water trench.
She ran out of the door. A motorbike had just stopped by the lines. It was Kannagi akka, the forest watcher, still in her khaki jacket. Mr Joseph was already talking at her about crackers.
'Akka,' said Selvi. 'They are not blocking us. They are calling someone. There were seven yesterday.'
'They have not made a sound in an hour,' said Mr Joseph.
'They have,' said Selvi. 'It is too low to hear. You can see it in a tumbler of water. And the big one's forehead shakes every time.'
Mr Joseph opened his mouth, but Kannagi akka held up her hand. She looked at the herd for a long moment, and then down the slope where they were looking.

'I have felt that in my chest,' she said quietly. 'Twice, in the forest. I did not know what it was.' She unhooked the radio from her belt. 'Nobody lights anything. I am going round by the lower path, well away from them. Selvi, go back inside.'
From the window Selvi watched three torches move along the bottom of the field. They stopped at the trench. Then one torch swung quickly from side to side.

The calf had been in the trench since the afternoon. The cement sides were as high as her back, and too smooth to climb. Every time the herd called, she had answered, and nobody on the hill had heard her either.
It took the forest staff forty minutes with crowbars and spades. They broke down one end of the trench and packed the earth into a slope. The calf scrambled up it on her knees and ran.

Everyone heard what came next. The herd roared and trumpeted, and made small chirping squeaks that Selvi had never heard an elephant make. The elephants closed round the calf until Selvi could not see her. Trunks touched her back, her ears and her mouth. Then the old female turned, and the whole herd went down to the stream with the calf in the middle.
The road was empty by eight. The night shift went to work.

Selvi came back to the window. The water in her tumbler was flat and still. For an hour the road outside had been full of calling, and the whole hill had heard only crickets. She drank the water and wondered what else was being said out there.
story.epiphany: The elephants were calling the whole time, in a voice too low for human ears. Selvi worked it out from what she could see and feel: the trembling forehead, the stillness afterwards, the direction they faced. A message can be there even when we hear nothing.
ask: Why might a very low call be useful to animals who live spread out in a forest?
What can you learn from which way an animal is facing and how still they are?
Name one message that might be passing near you now that your ears and eyes miss.
How could you test whether a sound too low to hear is really there?
When an animal's act looks stubborn or strange, what should you check before deciding why they did it?

roots.context: In the Ice and Prize Test you found out what a prize changes and what it leaves alone. You also met bees who dance directions and elephants who call below our hearing. Now we ask what this tells us about feeling, in you and in everyone else.

deep_truth.truth: In the Ice and Prize Test, most children hold the ice longer when the prize is bigger. The blink at a puff of air stays almost the same. A hermit crab also gives up a poor shell at a shock, but stays in a good one. So weighing a hurt against a want is a sign of feeling that anyone can see. An animal needs no cry and no face like ours to show it.
deep_truth.habit: We look for feelings in faces and cries, because that is how humans show them. So a crab, a fish or a bee, who has no face we can read and makes no cry we can hear, gets treated as if nothing were felt. This mixes up how a feeling is shown with whether the feeling is there.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Ice and Prize Test, the prize changed how long you held the ice, but hardly changed your blink. Hermit crabs left poor shells more readily than good ones at the same shock. Bumblebees accepted a hot feeder only when the sugar there was much sweeter.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who weighs a hurt against a want many times a day. A crab does that too, and so does a bee.
three.what_is_life: For anyone alive, some things are good for them and some are bad. Feelings are how that difference is known from the inside.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of messages that were not sent to us, such as dances in dark hives and rumbles below our hearing. Each kind of animal lives among their own.

roots.thread: Every animal alive today comes from the same early ancestors. Those ancestors already used chemicals such as serotonin to pass signals around their bodies. From that one beginning came many kinds of body: six legs and a brain the size of a sesame seed, a trunk and feet that listen, two hands and a voice. Feeling runs through all of them, and each body shows it in a different way. So when you watch a bee or an elephant weigh a choice, you are watching a relative do what you do.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased: all beings tremble at violence, and all fear death. Put yourself in the place of another, and do not harm or cause harm.
teachings.link: The verse asks you to work out another's feeling from your own. Scientists do the same when they compare a crab's trade-off with a person's. The verse simply does not wait for the experiment.

teachings.source: Tattvartha Sutra, chapter 2 (sutras 22 to 24 in most editions), a Jain text by Umasvati
teachings.teaching: Living beings are grouped by how many senses they have. Plants have one sense, touch. Worms have two, ants three, bees four, and humans and other large animals five.
teachings.link: This old list draws no line between beings who feel and beings who do not. It says they differ in how many ways they sense. Today's scientists also find that feeling is hard to switch off at any one kind of animal.

teachings.source: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), chapter 17, in a footnote
teachings.teaching: On how we should treat other animals, he wrote: 'The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?'
teachings.link: Bentham said that what matters is feeling, and that cleverness and speech are beside the point. The trade-off tests and mood tests in this lesson are ways of putting his question to a crab or a bee.

science.text: Crabs, bees and fish weigh harm against reward, which a simple reflex does not do.
Whether insects and crabs have conscious experience is argued over. The New York Declaration of 2024 calls it a realistic possibility.
Nobody can explain how the activity of nerve cells goes with a feeling, even in a human brain. David Chalmers named this the hard problem in 1995.

other_view.who: Joseph LeDoux, a brain scientist who has studied fear in rats for decades
other_view.view: The brain circuits that make an animal freeze or flee work without awareness, even in people. LeDoux thinks a felt emotion needs further brain parts that build a picture of oneself. So he says a rat who freezes may or may not feel afraid, and that behaviour cannot tell us which. This is a careful view from someone who knows the evidence well.

practice.title: Two pulls at once
practice.say: Sit still and breathe slowly. Think of something you want to do right now, such as scratch, get up or have a snack. Stay still for one minute anyway. Notice where in your body the wanting sits. Notice that something in you is weighing the want against staying still. Now look at any animal you can see, such as a crow, an ant or a person. Ask yourself quietly what two things they might be weighing right now.
practice.kid: Sit still. Think of something you want to do. Stay still for one minute anyway. Where in your body is the wanting? Now watch any animal nearby. What might they be weighing?

ask: When you weigh a hurt against a want, who or what is doing the weighing?
If a bee weighs heat against sugar, what do you and the bee have in common at that moment?
Could there be a feeling that never shows in anything an animal does? How would anyone know?

games.title: Stay or Leave? The hermit crab game
games.context: In this game you are a hermit crab in a shell. Each round something pinches you, and you choose to stay or to leave. You find out that the best choice depends on two things at once.

printables.title: 15 shell cards, each with the shell's worth on the back (three shells each worth 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5)
16 pinch cards, each with the pinch's strength on the back (from 0 to 4)
Score sheet for one player: six rounds

rules: Cut out the cards. Shuffle the shell cards and the pinch cards into two piles, with the worth and strength sides face down. Print them on two colours of paper if you can, so the piles do not get mixed.

Each player takes 12 dry beans or chana. These are your strength. Each player draws one shell card and turns it over. That is the shell you live in. A shell worth 5 is roomy and strong. A shell worth 1 is cramped and cracked.
Each round, turn over the top pinch card. The same pinch hits every player.

Now each player chooses. To stay, pay as many beans as the strength of the pinch. To leave, pay 2 beans, put your shell at the bottom of the shell pile and draw a new shell. Leaving costs beans because a crab with no shell is in danger.
If you do not have enough beans to stay, you must leave. If you have fewer than 2 beans, you lose the beans you have and keep your shell.
Play six rounds. Then score: multiply your shell's worth by 4, and add the beans you have left.
The highest score wins. If you play alone, try to beat 16 points.

setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the two piles. Give each player 12 beans and one shell card.

setup.art: A pinch card turned over showing 'Strength 3', and a player with a shell card showing 'Worth 2' thinking with a hand on her chin.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a pinch card. Look at your shell's worth.

setup.art: One player pushing three chana to the middle to stay, and another pushing two chana and drawing a new shell card.
setup.caption: 3. Stay and pay the pinch, or leave, pay 2 and draw a new shell.

setup.art: A score sheet with a sum written on it: 4 times 4 plus 5 equals 21.
setup.caption: 4. After six rounds, multiply your shell by 4 and add your beans.

flow.do: Cut out the 15 shell cards and 16 pinch cards. Shuffle each pile, with the worth and strength sides down. Give every player 12 beans, a score sheet and one shell card.
flow.say: Cut out the cards and shuffle the two piles. Take 12 beans and one shell each. Turn your shell over and read what it is worth.
flow.kid: Shuffle both piles. Take 12 beans and one shell. Turn your shell over.
flow.context: This is the first step of the hermit crab game. You set up the cards and beans.
flow.parent: Dry beans and chana can choke a child under five, so keep them away from small brothers and sisters. If you have no printer, write the cards on slips of paper. The backs are listed in the printables.

flow.do: Play rounds 1 to 3. Each round, turn over one pinch card. Each player says 'stay' or 'leave' and pays. After each round, each player says in one sentence why they chose that.
flow.say: Here is the pinch. Will you stay and pay, or leave, pay 2 and take a new shell? Tell me why.
flow.kid: Look at the pinch and your shell. Stay or leave? Say why.
flow.context: In this step you play the first three rounds and say why you chose each time.

ask.q: What two things did you look at before you chose?
good: How strong the pinch was and how good my shell was.
My shell's worth and my beans.
Only the pinch. I did not think about the shell.

flow.do: Play rounds 4 to 6. Then each player multiplies their shell's worth by 4 and adds their beans. Write the scores down.
flow.say: Three more rounds. Then multiply your shell's worth by 4 and add your beans.
flow.kid: Play three more rounds. Then work out your score.
flow.context: In this step you finish the game and work out the scores.
flow.parent: A player who always stays usually ends near 14 points. A player who always leaves ends near 12. A player who weighs the shell against the pinch usually scores about 19 or 20.

flow.do: Ask each player when they stayed and when they left. Then show the check question, which tells what real hermit crabs did in a test.
flow.say: When did you stay through a strong pinch? When did you leave at a weak one?
flow.kid: When did you stay? When did you leave?
flow.context: In this step you compare your choices with what real hermit crabs did in a test.

check.q: A crab in a good shell stays through a shock. A crab in a poor shell leaves at the same shock. What does this show?
options: The crab weighs the shock against the shell
The shock was weaker in the good shell
Crabs in good shells are asleep
check.why: The shock was the same. Only the worth of the shell changed. So the crab's choice depended on two things together, as yours did in the game. If you picked the second answer, look again: the scientists gave the same shock to both.

flow.think: Would a reaction that works like a knee kick ever depend on how good the shell is?

experiments.title: The Ice and Prize Test: what does a prize change?
experiments.context: In this test you hold an ice cube for as long as you choose, for no prize, a small prize and a big prize. Then you try to stop a blink for a prize. You find out which of the two a prize can change.
experiments.question: Does a bigger prize change how long you choose to hold an ice cube? Does a prize change whether you blink at a puff of air?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Will you hold the ice longer for a big prize than for no prize? Will a prize help you not to blink when air is puffed at your eye? Say why you think so for each one.
experiments.fair_test: Every ice cube comes from the same tray and goes straight from the freezer into the hand. You hold each cube the same way, in a closed fist over a bowl. You change hands each round and rest for three minutes, so a cold hand does not spoil the next round. The prize is said aloud before each round. The first and last rounds both have no prize. If those two times are close, the order of the rounds did not matter much. No round goes past 90 seconds.

materials.item: ice cubes of the same size, from one tray
a bowl and a small towel
a timer, such as the stopwatch on a phone
chana or dry beans to use as prize tokens
clean drinking straws, one for each person who puffs
the results table, drawn on paper, and a pencil

experiments.safety: Stop any round at 90 seconds, even if the child wants to go on. The child may let go at any moment, and letting go early is a useful result. Do not do the ice rounds with a child whose skin swells or itches in the cold, or whose fingers turn white in the cold. Puff the air gently from the side of the eye, from a hand's width away, and never push the straw towards the eye.

schedule.what: Guess, hold the ice for four rounds with rests, do the puff test, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Write the seconds held in each round. Under the table, write how many times you blinked in five puffs with no prize, and in five puffs with a prize. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Example: how long one child held the ice
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what a chart of results looks like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: A table with a tray of ice cubes, a bowl with a towel beside it, a phone showing a stopwatch and a small heap of chana.
setup.caption: 1. Set out the ice, bowl, towel, timer and tokens. Agree what the tokens buy.

setup.art: A child holding a closed fist over a bowl, with drops of water falling from it, while a parent watches a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Hold one ice cube in a closed fist over the bowl. Let go whenever you choose.

setup.art: A child rubbing one hand with a towel while the parent writes a number in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Write the seconds. Warm the hand and rest for three minutes. Change hands.

setup.art: A parent holding a straw a hand's width from the side of a child's open eye and blowing gently.
setup.caption: 4. Puff air gently at the side of the eye, five times. Count the blinks.

flow.do: Read the question aloud. Ask your child for both guesses and the reason for each. Write the guesses above the table. Do not say whether you agree.
flow.say: You will hold ice for no prize, a small prize and a big prize. Will the prize change how long you hold on? Why? Then I will puff air at your eye. Will a prize help you not to blink? Why?
flow.kid: Make two guesses, one for the ice and one for the blink. Say why for each.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ice and Prize Test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Which do you think a prize can change more, holding the ice or blinking? Why?
good: Holding, because I can decide to hold on.
Blinking just happens by itself.
Both, if the prize is big enough. We can test it.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children are sure a big prize will stop the blink.

flow.do: Agree what the tokens buy, and keep to it. For example, every 3 tokens buy one minute of a game your child chooses. Explain the rules. They may let go at any time, and no round goes past 90 seconds.
flow.say: Each token is worth something real. Let us agree what. You can let go whenever you want. This is not a test of how brave you are. It is a test of what a prize changes.
flow.kid: Agree what the tokens buy. You can let go any time. It is not a bravery test.
flow.context: In this step you agree on the prize and the safety rules for the Ice and Prize Test.
flow.parent: The prize must matter to your child, or the test shows nothing. Choose something you will really give. The most a child can win in the whole test is 46 tokens.

flow.do: Round 1 has no prize. Put one ice cube in your child's left hand. They close the fist over the bowl. Start the timer. Stop it when they let go, or at 90 seconds. Write the seconds. Then they dry and warm the hand for three minutes.
flow.say: Round 1. There is no prize this time. Hold the ice for as long as you choose. Let go when you want to.
flow.kid: Round 1 has no prize. Hold the ice as long as you choose. Then warm your hand.
flow.context: In this step you do the first round of the Ice and Prize Test, with no prize.
flow.parent: Say nothing while your child holds the ice. Do not count aloud or cheer, because that is a kind of prize too. During the rest, they can rub the hand on the towel or hold it under an arm.

flow.do: Round 2 uses the right hand. Say the prize first: 1 token for every full 10 seconds. Time it, write it and pay the tokens. Rest three minutes. Round 3 uses the left hand. The prize is 3 tokens for every full 10 seconds. Time it, write it, pay and rest.
flow.say: Round 2. You win 1 token for every 10 seconds you hold on. Go. Now rest. Round 3. This time you win 3 tokens for every 10 seconds.
flow.kid: Round 2 pays 1 token for every 10 seconds. Round 3 pays 3 tokens. Let go when you choose.
flow.context: In this step you do rounds 2 and 3 of the Ice and Prize Test, with a small prize and then a big prize.

check.q: Why do we rest and change hands between rounds?
options: So a cold, numb hand does not change the next result
So the ice has time to melt
So the child forgets the prize
check.why: A hand that is already cold feels the next cube differently. Resting and changing hands keeps each round as alike as possible, so that only the prize changes. If you picked 'melt', remember that each round starts with a fresh cube.

flow.parent: If your child reaches 90 seconds, stop the round and write '90, stopped'. Pay only for full 10 seconds held.

flow.do: Round 4 uses the right hand and has no prize, the same as round 1. Time it and write it. Then compare rounds 1 and 4.
flow.say: Last ice round. There is no prize again. Hold on for as long as you choose.
flow.kid: Round 4 has no prize again. Hold the ice as long as you choose.
flow.context: In this step you repeat the no-prize round of the Ice and Prize Test, to check whether the order of the rounds mattered.
flow.parent: If rounds 1 and 4 are close, then practice and cold hands did not change much. Any big difference in rounds 2 and 3 came from the prize. If round 4 is much longer than round 1, your child got used to the ice, and the test is less clear.

flow.do: Now the puff test. Your child keeps both eyes open. Puff gently through the straw at the outer corner of one eye, five times. Count the blinks. Then offer 2 tokens for every puff with no blink. Puff five more times and count again.
flow.say: Keep your eyes open. I will puff air five times. Now the prize: 2 tokens for every puff where you do not blink. Try your hardest.
flow.kid: Keep your eyes open while air is puffed. Then try not to blink for a prize.
flow.context: In this step of the Ice and Prize Test you find out whether a prize can stop a blink.
flow.parent: Hold the straw a hand's width from the side of the eye and blow one short, gentle puff. Most children blink at nearly every puff, with or without the prize. A few manage to hold back once or twice. Write down exactly what happened.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what the prize changed and what it did not. They write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Give the explanation in the parent note only after they have finished.
flow.say: Look at your numbers. What did the prize change? What did it leave almost the same? Write what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the Ice and Prize Test show.

ask.q: What did the prize change, and what did it hardly change?
good: I held the ice longer for the big prize.
I blinked almost every time, even for the prize.
The two no-prize rounds were close, so the prize made the difference.

ask.q: Scientists gave hermit crabs a small shock in a good shell or a poor shell. Which is that more like, the ice or the puff? Why?
good: The ice, because the crab's choice changed with how good the shell was.
The ice, because both weigh a hurt against something they want.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. A blink at a puff of air is a reflex, a fast reaction that happens the same way each time. Letting go of the ice is different, because how long you held on depended on what you could gain. Scientists use the same idea with other animals. If your child held to 90 seconds in every round, the limit hid the result, and that is worth saying. Do not make the limit longer. If your child held back some blinks, say so honestly. A reflex can sometimes be held back a little, but far less than a choice can be changed.
flow.think: A bumblebee walks onto a hot feeder only when the sugar there is much sweeter. What might be going on in the bee?

experiments.title: The Floor Message Test: can a message travel through the ground?
experiments.context: In this test one person sends soft thumps along the floor, and a listener three metres away tries to read them. You compare listening with your ears in the air, with an ear on the floor, and with your bare feet. You will find out whether feet can catch what ears miss, as elephants do when they feel each other's rumbles through the ground.
experiments.question: Can a message of soft thumps reach a listener through the floor when it is too soft to hear through the air? Which works best: ears in the air, an ear on the floor, or bare feet?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Which way of listening will get the most messages right, and which the fewest? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same person sends every message, with the pad of one finger, at the same soft strength. The listener is always three metres away with eyes shut. The room is quiet, with the fan and the television off. A die chooses each message, so the sender cannot fall into a pattern. Each way of listening gets six messages. Only the way of listening changes.

materials.item: a quiet room with a hard floor of tile, stone or cement, and three metres of clear space
a die
a towel or mat to lie on
a measuring tape, or count ten of the child's foot lengths
the results table, drawn on paper, and a pencil

experiments.safety: Lie down away from doors that someone might open. If people live below you, keep the thumps as soft as the test asks.

schedule.what: Guess, find the right soft thump, send six messages for each way of listening, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: For each message, write the thumps sent, the thumps the listener said, and right or wrong. Count the right answers out of six for each way of listening. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
