data.label: Sitting, bare feet on the floor

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show what a chart of results looks like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: Two people at opposite ends of a tiled room, three metres apart, one crouching with a finger on the floor and one standing with eyes shut.
setup.caption: 1. Sender and listener stand three metres apart. The listener shuts their eyes.

setup.art: A hand rolling a die beside a finger pad thumping softly on a floor tile.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die to choose 1, 2 or 3 thumps. Thump softly with the pad of one finger.

setup.art: A child lying on a towel with one ear pressed to the floor and the other ear covered by a hand.
setup.caption: 3. Listen three ways: standing, with an ear on the floor, and sitting with bare feet flat.

setup.art: A results table with three rows of ticks and crosses and a total out of six beside each row.
setup.caption: 4. Count the right answers out of six for each way.

flow.do: Read the question. Ask your child which way of listening will work best and worst, and why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will send soft thumps along the floor. You will listen standing, with an ear on the floor, and with bare feet. Which will work best? Which worst? Why?
flow.kid: Which way of listening will work best? Which worst? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Floor Message Test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Why might a sound travel differently through a floor than through air?
good: The floor is hard, so the shaking passes along it.
Air is loose, so a soft sound dies away.
I am not sure. We can test it.

flow.do: Find the right thump. The listener stands three metres away with eyes shut. The sender thumps the floor with one finger pad, softer each time. Stop when the standing listener is no longer sure whether there was a thump. Use that strength for the whole test.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Tell me each time you hear a thump. I will make them softer and softer.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Say when you hear a thump. They will get softer.
flow.context: In this step of the Floor Message Test you find a thump soft enough to be hard to hear through the air.
flow.parent: This step matters most. If the thump is easy to hear standing up, every way of listening will score six and the test shows nothing. Use the soft pad of the finger, not the nail or the knuckle. Switch off the fan.

flow.do: The listener stands with eyes shut. Roll the die. For 1 or 2, send one thump. For 3 or 4, send two. For 5 or 6, send three. Leave one second between thumps. The listener says the number. Write it down. Do this six times.
flow.say: Stand still with your eyes shut. I will send one, two or three thumps. Tell me how many. If you are not sure, guess.
flow.kid: Stand with your eyes shut. How many thumps were there? Guess if you are not sure.
flow.context: In this step of the Floor Message Test the listener stands, with ears in the air.
flow.parent: Do not say whether each answer is right until all six are done. A listener who is only guessing gets about two right out of six.

flow.do: The listener lies on the towel with one ear pressed to the floor. They cover the other ear with a hand. Send six more messages chosen by the die. Write each answer.
flow.say: Now lie down and press one ear to the floor. Cover your other ear. How many thumps this time?
flow.kid: Lie down. Press one ear to the floor. Cover the other ear. How many thumps?
flow.context: In this step of the Floor Message Test the listener presses an ear to the floor.

check.q: Why does a die choose the number of thumps?
options: So the listener cannot guess from a pattern
So the thumps are louder
So the test is quicker
check.why: People who make up messages fall into patterns, such as 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3. A listener could then be right without hearing anything. The die removes that. If you picked 'louder', remember that the strength stays the same for the whole test.

flow.do: The listener sits on a chair with bare feet flat on the floor and both hands pressed over the ears. Send six more messages chosen by the die. Write each answer.
flow.say: Now sit with your bare feet flat on the floor. Press your hands over your ears. Can your feet tell how many thumps?
flow.kid: Sit with bare feet flat. Cover both ears. Can your feet feel the thumps?
flow.context: In this step of the Floor Message Test the listener uses bare feet, with both ears covered.
flow.parent: Most people feel little or nothing through their feet at this strength. That is a real result. Write down what your child says.

flow.do: Count the right answers for each way. Ask your child what the numbers show, and why they think it happened. They write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Then read them the parent note.
flow.say: Count the right answers in each row. Which way of listening worked best? Was any way no better than guessing? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: Count your right answers for each way. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results of the Floor Message Test show.

ask.q: A listener who only guesses gets about 2 right out of 6. Which of your rows could be just guessing?
good: Standing, because I got 2.
My feet row, because 3 is close to 2.
Not the ear on the floor, because I got all 6.

ask.q: Your feet felt little. An elephant's feet pick up rumbles from far away. What might be different about her feet?
good: They are much bigger.
She may have more nerve endings for shaking.
She is very heavy, so her feet press hard on the ground.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. A soft thump shakes the floor, and a hard floor passes that shaking along well. Air passes on far less of it. With an ear on the floor, the shaking goes through the skull bones to the inner ear. An elephant's foot has a thick cushion of fat and many nerve endings for pressure. Scientists think the shaking may also travel up her leg bones to her ears. Our feet have far fewer of those nerve endings.
flow.think: When might the ground be a better way to send a message than the air?

activities.title: Read the Dance: where did the bee send her sisters?
activities.context: In this activity you find out how a honeybee tells her sisters where the flowers are, by working out the code of her waggle dance from three examples. Then you use it to mark on a map where three dancers found food.

materials.item: plain paper
a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: Keep the map with the hive, the sun arrow and the three flower marks. Under it, write the rule for direction and the rule for distance in your own words.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a circle for the comb, the word 'up' at the top, and a wavy line pointing straight up from the centre, labelled '2 seconds'.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three dance cards: a circle, the word 'up', and a wavy line for the waggle run.

setup.art: A second sheet with a small hive drawn in the middle and a sun drawn at the top edge, with an arrow from the hive to the sun.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a map: the hive in the middle and the sun at the top edge.

setup.art: A child measuring 6 centimetres from the hive towards the sun with a ruler and drawing a flower there.
setup.caption: 3. Decode each dance and mark the flowers on the map.

flow.do: Draw dance card A. It is a circle with 'up' written at the top and a wavy line from the centre straight up, marked '2 seconds'. Tell your child what bee A did and where her food was. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: A bee found flowers and came home. On the comb she ran straight up, waggling for 2 seconds. Her flowers were towards the sun, about 2 kilometres away. What do you notice? What might the run mean?
flow.kid: Bee A ran straight up for 2 seconds. Her food was towards the sun. What might the run mean?
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Dance. You look at one dance and wonder what it means.

ask.q: What do you notice, and what do you wonder?
good: Up might mean towards the sun.
Two seconds might mean two kilometres.
How do the other bees see her in the dark?

flow.do: Draw card B with a wavy line straight down, marked '3 seconds'. Say that this food was directly away from the sun, about 3 kilometres off. Then draw card C with a line pointing to the right, marked '1 second'. Ask where bee C's food is.
flow.say: Bee B ran straight down for 3 seconds. Her food was away from the sun, about 3 kilometres off. Bee C ran to the right for 1 second. Where is her food? Tell me your rule.
flow.kid: Bee B ran down for 3 seconds. Her food was away from the sun. Where is bee C's food?
flow.context: In this step of Read the Dance you work out the code from two examples and try it on a third.

ask.q: What is the rule for direction, and the rule for distance?
good: Up on the comb means towards the sun, and the same turn from up means the same turn from the sun.
Each second of waggling is about one kilometre.

flow.parent: Bee C's food is to the right of the sun's direction, a quarter turn, about 1 kilometre away. Let your child say a rule before you confirm it. One second for one kilometre is a rough figure for the honeybees Karl von Frisch studied.

flow.do: Draw the map: a hive in the middle and the sun at the top edge. On this map 3 centimetres stand for 1 kilometre. Your child marks the flowers of bees A, B and C with a ruler. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is the hive, and the sun is this way. On our map, 3 centimetres is 1 kilometre. Mark where each bee's flowers are.
flow.kid: Mark each bee's flowers on the map. Use 3 centimetres for each kilometre.
flow.context: In this step of Read the Dance you use the code to mark three flower patches on a map.

check.q: A dancer runs to the left of straight up, a quarter turn, for 2 seconds. Where is her food?
options: A quarter turn left of the sun, about 2 kilometres away
Straight towards the sun, about 2 kilometres away
On the left side of the hive, very near
check.why: The turn from 'up' on the comb equals the turn from the sun outside, and 2 seconds means about 2 kilometres. If you picked the third answer, remember that the dance is about a far place outside, not about a spot on the comb.

flow.parent: Bee A's flowers go 6 centimetres towards the sun. Bee B's go 9 centimetres directly away from it. Bee C's go 3 centimetres to the right. Honeybees do this in the dark, by touch.
flow.think: 'Up' does not look like the sun. How might bees have come to share the same rule?

activities.title: Saw or Guessed? Ten minutes with one animal
activities.context: In this activity you watch one animal for ten minutes. You write what they did in one column and what you guess they felt or wanted in another. You will find out how much of what we say about an animal we really saw. Scientists who study animal behaviour keep these two apart.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a timer
one animal you can watch without disturbing, such as a crow, a pigeon, a line of ants, a house gecko, a street dog seen from a window, or a pet

activities.safety: Watch street dogs and monkeys only from a window or balcony. Do not touch or feed the animal during the ten minutes.
activities.record: Keep the two-column page. Circle one guess, and write under it another explanation and what you would watch for next.

setup.art: A notebook page ruled into two columns headed 'What I saw' and 'What I guess', with a pencil across it.
setup.caption: 1. Rule two columns: 'What I saw' and 'What I guess'.

setup.art: A child sitting quietly at a window with a notebook, watching a crow on the grill.
setup.caption: 2. Watch one animal for ten minutes without disturbing them.

setup.art: A notebook line reading 'hopped back when the pigeon landed' in one column and 'did not want to share?' in the other.
setup.caption: 3. Write each act on the left. Write your guess about it on the right.

flow.do: Rule a page into two columns. Head them 'What I saw' and 'What I guess'. Choose one animal you can see now. Start a ten-minute timer.
flow.say: Pick one animal to watch. In the first column write only what a camera would record. In the second, write what you guess they felt or wanted.
flow.kid: Pick one animal. Write what you see on the left. Write your guesses on the right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Saw or Guessed. You set up the page and choose an animal.
flow.parent: If no other animal is about, your child can watch a person in the family who agrees to be watched. Humans are animals too, and the same two columns work.

flow.do: Watch for ten minutes. Each time the animal does something new, your child writes it on the left. Then they write a guess on the right, if they have one. Stay quiet and still.
flow.say: Watch quietly. Each time they do something new, write it down. If you have a guess about why, write that in the other column.
flow.kid: Watch quietly for ten minutes. Write each new thing they do. Add your guess beside it.
flow.context: In this step of Saw or Guessed you watch one animal and fill in the two columns.
flow.parent: Look for words such as 'angry', 'happy', 'bored' or 'wants' in the left column. Those are guesses. Ask what your child saw that made them think so, and move the word across.

flow.do: Your child circles one guess. Under it they write one other explanation for the same act. Then they write what they would watch for next to decide between the two.
flow.say: Circle one of your guesses. What else could explain what you saw? What would you look for next time to find out which is right?
flow.kid: Circle one guess. Write one other explanation. What would you watch for next?
flow.context: In this step of Saw or Guessed you test one of your guesses by thinking of another explanation.

check.q: Which of these is something seen, and not a guess?
options: The crow dropped the bread and flew off when the cat came
The crow was scared of the cat
The crow did not like the bread
check.why: A camera could record the bread dropping and the crow flying. 'Scared' and 'did not like' are guesses about what went on inside. They may well be right, but they need evidence, and the first sentence is that evidence.

flow.think: Your guesses about a friend's feelings are guesses too. What makes you trust them?

activities.title: The Middle Note: how a mood test for bees works
activities.context: In this activity you learn that one note means a sweet and another note means something bitter. Then you hear a note in between and choose what to do, so you find out what you expect when a sign is unclear. Scientists used a test like this to find out whether shaken honeybees expect the worst.

materials.item: steel tumblers of the same size
water
a steel spoon
raisins or small pieces of jaggery
methi seeds, which are bitter, or small pieces of raw bitter gourd
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Check that your child can safely eat the raisins and the methi seeds. If you prefer, the bitter note can cost one raisin from their pile, with nothing bitter to eat.
activities.record: Write what you did each time the middle note sounded: reached or held back. Write one sentence about what you think decided it.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers in a row, one full of water, one half full and one empty, with a spoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one tumbler, half fill another and leave one empty. Strike each one gently on the rim.

setup.art: A child sitting with her back turned and one hand held out, while a parent strikes the full tumbler with a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. The child turns away. One note means a raisin. The other means a bitter seed.

setup.art: A parent striking the half-full tumbler while the child hesitates with her hand half raised.
setup.caption: 3. Now sound the middle note. Does the child reach or hold back?

flow.do: Fill one tumbler to the top, half fill the second and leave the third empty. Strike each on the rim with the spoon. Your child listens and says which note is highest and which is lowest. Put the half-full tumbler out of sight.
flow.say: Listen to the three tumblers. Which note is highest? Which is lowest? Is the half-full one in between?
flow.kid: Listen to the three tumblers. Which note is highest? Which is lowest?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Middle Note. You make three notes with tumblers and water.
flow.parent: A struck tumbler gives a lower note when it holds more water. Check that the half-full note sounds in between. If the notes are hard to tell apart, use bigger tumblers or glasses.

flow.do: Your child turns away. Strike the full tumbler. If they hold out a hand, they get a raisin. Strike the empty tumbler. If they hold out a hand, they get a methi seed to chew. Mix the two notes eight times.
flow.say: Turn round. When you hear a note, you may hold out your hand or not. One note brings a raisin. The other brings a bitter seed. Work out which is which.
flow.kid: Turn round. One note brings a raisin. The other brings a bitter seed. Hold out your hand, or not.
flow.context: In this step of The Middle Note you learn which note means sweet and which means bitter.
flow.parent: Most children stop reaching for the bitter note within four or five tries. Carry on until they get two of each right in a row.

flow.do: Carry on mixing the two notes. Among them, strike the hidden half-full tumbler three times. Give nothing for that note. Write down whether your child reached or held back each time.
flow.say: Keep going. Hold out your hand or not, as you choose.
flow.kid: Keep going. Hold out your hand, or not. You choose.
flow.context: In this step of The Middle Note you hear an in-between note and choose what to do.
flow.parent: Do not warn your child that a new note is coming. Their first reaction to it is the result.

flow.do: Show the third tumbler. Ask your child what they did at the middle note and why. Then tell them about the honeybee test.
flow.say: There was a third note in between. What did you do when you heard it? Why? Scientists did this with honeybees and smells. Bees who had just been shaken held back more at the in-between smell.
flow.kid: There was a middle note. What did you do at that note? Why?
flow.context: In this step of The Middle Note you compare your choice with what honeybees did in a real test.

check.q: Shaken bees treated an in-between smell as bitter more often than calm bees. What does this suggest?
options: A bad experience left the bees expecting worse
Shaken bees lost their sense of smell
Bees prefer bitter drinks
check.why: The shaken bees still told the sweet smell from the bitter one, so their sense of smell was working. What changed was how they took an unclear sign. In people, that pattern goes with a low or worried mood.

flow.parent: Your child's three tries say nothing about their mood. Scientists compare many animals in each group. The activity only shows how the test works.
flow.think: What kind of day might make you take an unclear message as bad news?

activities.title: The Evidence Checklist: reflex, or more than a reflex?
activities.context: In this activity you check six real findings about animals against a list of four signs. You will find out how to tell a simple reflex from something more. Scientists use lists like this when they ask whether an animal feels pain.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a ruler

activities.record: Keep the table of six findings and four signs, with your ticks. Under it, write which finding you think is the strongest evidence and why.

setup.art: A hand-ruled table with six rows and four columns headed 'guards the hurt place', 'learns to avoid', 'weighs it against a reward' and 'eased by a painkiller'.
setup.caption: 1. Rule a table: six rows for findings and four columns for signs.

setup.art: A child reading a finding aloud from a list while pointing at a row of the table.
setup.caption: 2. Read each finding. Tick every sign that the finding shows.

setup.art: A finished table with different numbers of ticks in each row and one row circled.
setup.caption: 3. Count the ticks. Circle the finding you think is the strongest evidence.

flow.do: Rule a table with four columns. Head them 'guards the hurt place', 'learns to avoid', 'weighs it against a reward' and 'eased by a painkiller'. Ask your child why each sign might matter.
flow.say: Here are four signs scientists look for. Why might each one tell us more than a simple flinch does?
flow.kid: Here are four signs. Why might each one tell us more than a flinch?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Evidence Checklist. You draw the table of four signs.

ask.q: Why would a painkiller making a difference be a clue?
good: If the medicine that eases our pain also changes what the animal does, something similar may be going on.
A flinch would still happen with a painkiller.

flow.do: Read the six findings in the parent note aloud, one at a time. For each, your child writes a short name in a row and ticks every sign it shows.
flow.say: Listen to each finding. Tick each sign that it shows. Some will get one tick, and some will get more.
flow.kid: Listen to each finding. Tick every sign it shows.
flow.context: In this step of The Evidence Checklist you check six real findings against the four signs.
flow.parent: Read these out. 1. A trout with a sore lip rubs it on the gravel, and feeds again sooner after a painkiller. 2. A hermit crab leaves a poor shell at a shock, but stays in a good one. 3. An octopus with a sore arm strokes it with her beak, avoids the room where it happened, and chooses a room where she got a painkiller. 4. A bumblebee walks onto a hot feeder only when the sugar there is much sweeter. 5. Your leg kicks when the knee is tapped. 6. A shore crab stops using a dark shelter where they got shocks.

flow.do: Count the ticks in each row. Ask your child which finding is the strongest evidence, and which tells us least. Ask what test they would add for the animal with fewest ticks.
flow.say: Which finding has the most ticks? For an animal with few ticks, what would you test next?
flow.kid: Which finding is the strongest? What would you test next?
flow.context: In this step of The Evidence Checklist you compare the findings and plan one more test.

check.q: Which finding shows only a reflex, with none of the four signs?
options: The leg kicks when the knee is tapped
The crab leaves a poor shell but stays in a good one
The octopus chooses the room with the painkiller
check.why: The knee kick happens the same way each time. Nothing is guarded, learned or weighed, and no reward changes it. The crab weighed the shock against the shell, and the octopus sought out relief.

flow.parent: Likely ticks: the trout guards and is eased by a painkiller. The hermit crab weighs. The octopus guards, learns and is eased. The bumblebee weighs. The knee kick has none. The shore crab learns. Few ticks often mean that nobody has run that test yet. They do not mean the animal failed it.
flow.think: No list of signs can be complete. What sign would you add?

projects.title: One Neighbour, Five Days: what changes how they act?
projects.context: In this project you watch the same animal, or the same kind of animal, for ten minutes a day over five days. You look for what changes how they act, and you end with one claim and the evidence for it.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a timer
a window, balcony or doorstep from which you can see the same animals each day

projects.safety: Watch from a window, balcony or doorstep. Do not go near street dogs, monkeys or nesting birds, and do not feed them for this project.

schedule.what: Choose your neighbour and a time of day. Watch for ten minutes and list what they do.
Watch at the same time. Write what happened just before each change in what they did.
Watch again. Mark any act you have now seen on three days.
Watch again. Write one guess about what they want or feel, and what you saw that supports it.
Watch once more to check your guess. Write your claim, your evidence and one other explanation.

projects.record: Each day, write the date, the time, the weather, what the animal did, and what happened just before. On day 5, write one claim, the evidence from at least three days, and one other explanation that could also fit.

setup.art: A child at a balcony grill with a notebook, watching two crows on a neem tree at the same time each morning.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one animal neighbour and one time of day.

setup.art: A notebook page with rows for date, time, weather, 'what they did' and 'what happened just before'.
setup.caption: 2. Each day write what they did, and what happened just before.

setup.art: A notebook page headed 'My claim' with three short lines of evidence and a line headed 'Another explanation'.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, write one claim, your evidence and another explanation.

flow.do: Choose an animal who is there most days, such as crows, pigeons, sparrows, mynas, ants or a street dog. Choose a time. Watch for ten minutes. Your child lists everything the animal does, in plain words.
flow.say: Who will be your neighbour for five days? Watch for ten minutes. Write down each thing they do, the way a camera would see it.
flow.kid: Choose one animal neighbour. Watch for ten minutes. List what they do.
flow.context: This is day 1 of One Neighbour, Five Days. You choose an animal and list what they do.
flow.parent: Ants at a crack or pigeons on a ledge are there in almost every flat. If the animal does not appear one day, write that down. It is a result as well.

flow.do: On days 2, 3 and 4, watch at the same time for ten minutes. Each day your child writes what the animal did and what happened just before. On day 4 they write one guess about what the animal wants or feels.
flow.say: Same time, same place. What did they do today? What happened just before? By day 4, write one guess about what they want or feel.
flow.kid: Watch at the same time each day. Write what they did and what happened just before. On day 4, add one guess.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of One Neighbour, Five Days. You look for what changes the way the animal acts.
flow.wait: Do this once a day for three days
flow.parent: Help your child look for pairs, such as 'a kite flew over, and all the pigeons left the ledge'. An event followed by the same act on several days is good evidence.

flow.do: On day 5, watch once more to check the guess. Then your child writes a claim, the evidence from at least three days, and one other explanation. They tell the family what they found.
flow.say: Does today fit your guess? Write your claim and the evidence for it. Then write one other way to explain what you saw.
flow.kid: Check your guess today. Write your claim and your evidence. Write one other explanation.
flow.context: This is day 5 of One Neighbour, Five Days. You write your claim, your evidence and another explanation.

check.q: On three mornings, pigeons left the ledge just after a kite flew over. What is the most careful claim?
options: Pigeons on this ledge leave when a kite flies over
Pigeons hate kites
Pigeons are the most nervous birds
check.why: The first claim says only what was seen on three days. 'Hate' is a guess about a feeling, and it may be true, but the notes do not show it yet. The third claim compares pigeons with birds that were never watched.

flow.think: After five days, do you think your neighbour noticed you?

challenges.title: Ask Without Words: design a test of what an animal wants
challenges.context: In this challenge you design a test that lets an animal show which of two things they want, and how much. Marian Stamp Dawkins did this with hens in the 1970s.
challenges.problem: Pigeons or crows visit your window ledge. You want to find out which of two plain foods they prefer, and how strongly. You cannot ask them. Design a fair test in which the birds answer by what they do.
constraints: Use only plain foods that are safe for birds, such as uncooked rice, bajra or ragi grains, or unsalted puffed rice. No fried, salted or sweet food.
The test must show how much the birds want a food, as well as which food they choose.
The side each food is on must be chosen by a coin, so that the side cannot explain the result.
Plan at least 10 tries, and feed only a spoonful each time.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
two shallow lids or bowls of the same kind
a coin
two kinds of plain grain, a spoonful of each

general: Put two bowls side by side, one food in each, and count which bowl the birds visit first.
Swap the sides with a coin toss before every try.
Count how many of 10 tries each food wins.
creative: Make the favourite food cost more. Move that bowl closer to where you sit, and see how near the birds will come for it.
Cover the favourite food with a paper lid that the bird has to push off, and see whether they still choose it.
Offer a big pile of the second-choice food against a few grains of the favourite, and see where the choice flips.
Run the test in the morning and in the afternoon, to see whether hunger changes the answer.
challenges.your_turn: Design a test of what someone wants for a different animal, such as ants, a pet, or a baby cousin who cannot talk yet. Say what the two choices are, how you make one of them cost more, and how many tries you need.

setup.art: A sketch of a window ledge with two identical lids of grain and a coin drawn between them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the test: two foods, two bowls and a coin to choose the sides.

setup.art: A sketch showing one bowl moved step by step closer to a seated child, with distances marked.
setup.caption: 2. Add a cost: make the favourite food harder to get, step by step.

setup.art: A family member crouching like a bird and choosing between two bowls while the child writes a tally.
setup.caption: 3. Try your plan on a family member who plays the bird.

flow.do: Ask your child how a bird could show which food they prefer. Then ask what else, besides liking the food, could make a bird go to one bowl. Write the list.
flow.say: How could a bird tell you which food they like, without words? What else might make them pick one bowl, apart from the food in it?
flow.kid: How could a bird show which food they like, without using words?
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask Without Words. You list what could decide a bird's choice.

ask.q: What could make a bird choose a bowl, apart from the food?
good: It is nearer to where they landed.
It is farther from me.
They went there last time.
The pile looks bigger.

flow.do: Your child makes a plan that deals with each thing on the list. They can draw it, or set out the bowls and coin and explain it aloud. Then they add a cost. They choose a way to make the favourite food harder to get, in three steps.
flow.say: Show me your test, in a drawing or with the bowls. How will you stop the side from deciding it? Now make the favourite food cost more. How far will they go for it?
flow.kid: Draw your test, or set out the bowls and tell it. Fix each problem on your list. Then make the favourite food harder to get.
flow.context: In this step of Ask Without Words you draw a plan and add a cost to one choice.
flow.parent: A good plan has the same bowls, a coin for the sides and equal piles. The cost can be distance from a person, a paper lid to push off, or a smaller pile. The idea of a cost comes from this lesson's trade-off tests.

flow.do: A family member plays the bird. They secretly choose a favourite and how much they want it. Your child runs six tries of the plan and works out the favourite and how strong it is.
flow.say: I will be the bird. I have a favourite food, and I will not tell you. Run your test and find out what I want, and how much.
flow.kid: A family member plays the bird. Run your test. Find out what they want, and how much.
flow.context: In this step of Ask Without Words you try your plan on a family member who plays the bird.

check.q: A bird picks ragi over rice when both are near. She picks rice when the ragi is close to a person. What does this show?
options: She prefers ragi, but not enough to come near a person
She cannot tell ragi from rice
She prefers rice
check.why: With no cost, she chose ragi, so ragi is her favourite. When ragi cost her a risk, she gave it up. That tells you how much the ragi matters to her. Her choice changed with the cost, so she weighed the two.

flow.do: Your child fixes one weak point that the practice run showed. They write the final plan in five lines. If birds do visit your ledge, they may run it over the next few days.
flow.say: What went wrong in the practice run? Fix that one thing. Then write your final plan in five lines.
flow.kid: Fix one thing that went wrong. Write your final plan in five lines.
flow.context: In this step of Ask Without Words you improve your plan and write it out.
flow.parent: If your child runs the real test, keep to a spoonful of grain a day, so that the birds do not come to depend on it. Wash hands after handling the bowls.

items.p: On the comb, a honeybee runs straight up while waggling. Where is the food?
opts: In the direction of the sun
At the top of the hive
items.why: Straight up on the comb stands for 'towards the sun'. The dance is about a place outside, so the second answer mixes up the comb with the world. Straight down would mean away from the sun.

items.p: What does a longer waggle run tell the bees who follow the dancer?
items.why: The length of the waggle stands for distance. A bee who flew farther waggles for longer on each run.

items.p: Honeybees usually dance in the dark, so the followers read the dance by touch.
items.why: True. Inside a hive or a tree hollow there is almost no light. The followers stay close to the dancer and touch her with their antennae.

items.p: Sound that is too low for human ears is called ____.
items.why: Infrasound is lower than about 20 vibrations each second. The lowest part of an elephant's rumble is infrasound.

items.p: Why can a very low rumble keep a spread-out elephant family in touch?
opts: Low sounds travel farther than high sounds
Only elephants can make low sounds
items.why: Low sounds lose less energy to the air and bend around trees and hills. So they carry much farther than high sounds of the same loudness.

items.p: If people nearby hear nothing, the elephants are not calling.
items.why: False. Much of a rumble is below human hearing. Katy Payne first noticed the calls as a throbbing in the air, and special recorders confirmed them.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a body and brain state that can be measured
what that state is like from inside
a fast reaction that is the same each time
giving up one thing to get more of another
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: An emotion can be measured from outside. A feeling is known from inside. A reflex does not change with what else matters, and a trade-off does.

items.p: Sort each one: can it be measured from outside, or is it known only from inside?
items: a stress chemical in the blood
how sweet jaggery tastes to you
items.a: as given
items.why: Heartbeats, acts and chemicals can be measured by someone else. What an experience is like is known directly only by the one who has it.

items.p: In a test, you hold ice longer for a big prize than for no prize. What does that show?
opts: Letting go was weighed against the prize
The ice was warmer in the big-prize round
items.why: The ice was the same. Only the prize changed, and your time changed with it. So letting go was a choice that weighed discomfort against gain. A reflex would not change with the prize.

items.p: A blink at a puff of air changes a lot when a prize is offered.
items.why: False. The blink is a reflex. It happens almost every time, prize or no prize. That is what makes it different from a weighed choice.

items.p: A crab leaves a poor shell at a shock, but stays in a good one. This weighing is called a ____.
items.why: The crab weighs the shock against the worth of the shell. That weighing is called a trade-off.

items.p: Explain why scientists do not count a flinch alone as evidence that an animal feels pain.
items.a: A flinch can be a reflex, which happens the same way whatever else is going on. Scientists look for more, such as guarding the hurt place, learning to avoid the cause, or weighing the hurt against a reward.
items.why: A strong answer says that a reflex needs no weighing, and names at least one further sign that scientists look for.

items.p: Which is something you saw, and not a guess about a feeling?
opts: The dog lowered her tail and backed away
The dog wanted to say sorry
items.why: A camera could record the tail and the backing away. 'Ashamed' and 'wanted to say sorry' are guesses about what went on inside her.

items.p: A pigeon flies off the ledge when you open the window. Write what you saw. Then write two possible explanations.
items.a: Seen: the pigeon flew off just as the window opened. Explanations: the sudden noise or movement frightened the pigeon, or the pigeon was about to leave anyway.
items.why: A strong answer keeps the act separate from the guesses, and gives two different explanations for the same act.

items.p: Draw a waggle dance that sends bees a quarter turn to the right of the sun, far away. Label the run.
items.a: A comb with 'up' marked, and a long wavy run pointing to the right, a quarter turn from up. The label says the run is long because the food is far.
items.why: A strong drawing points the run to the right of 'up' by a quarter turn, and makes it long to show a far place.

items.p: Bees flew a few metres through a narrow patterned tunnel, then danced for a far place. Why?
opts: The pattern rushed past their eyes
They forgot where they had been
items.why: A bee measures distance by how much scenery streams past her eyes. In a narrow patterned tunnel a lot streams past in a short flight, so she measures 'far'.

items.p: In India, the dwarf honeybee dances on the flat top of her comb and points straight at the food.
items.why: True. Her comb is in the open, so she can dance on a flat surface and aim her run at the food. Bees who dance on an upright comb use the 'up means sun' code.

items.p: Put in order how scientists showed that bees use the danced direction.
a: Bees followed a dance in the hive
Scientists fixed tiny radar aerials on the followers
They carried the followers to a new starting spot
The bees flew the danced direction and distance from there
The bees arrived at the wrong place, so smell was not guiding them
items.why: Moving the bees separated the dance message from the smell of the real flowers. The bees followed the message.

items.p: Recorded rumbles were played into the ground only. Elephants bunched together and faced the source. What does this show?
opts: Elephants can pick up signals through the ground
items.why: Nothing was played through the air, and the elephants still responded. So the message reached them through the ground.

items.p: A listener gets 2 of 6 messages right standing, and 6 of 6 with an ear on the floor. How many more?
items.why: 6 take away 2 is 4. With three possible messages, guessing alone gives about 2 right out of 6. So the standing score is no better than guessing.

items.p: Sort each one: a reflex, or a weighed choice?
items: a knee kick when the knee is tapped
a blink at a puff of air
a crab leaving a poor shell but not a good one
a bee accepting heat for sweeter sugar
holding ice longer for a bigger prize
items.a: as given
items.why: The reflexes happen the same way each time. The weighed choices change when the reward changes.

items.p: A child holds ice 20 seconds for no prize and 60 seconds for a big prize. How many times as long?
items.why: 60 divided by 20 is 3. The child held on three times as long for the big prize. The ice did not change, so the prize made the difference.

items.p: Why does the ice test start and end with a no-prize round?
opts: To check whether the order of rounds mattered
To give the child more practice
items.why: If the first and last rounds give close times, then cold hands and practice did not change much. Any big change in the middle rounds came from the prize.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Guards a sore place. Learns to avoid harm. Flinches. Accepts harm for reward.
items.a: Flinches. A flinch can be a reflex. The other three need more than a reflex.
items.why: Guarding, learning and weighing all change with the situation. A flinch happens the same way each time.

items.p: Shaken honeybees could no longer tell the sweet smell from the bitter smell.
items.why: False. They still told the two apart. What changed was how they treated in-between smells. They took those as bitter more often.

items.p: A crayfish who got shocks stays in the dark. A calming medicine sends them back to the light. What does this suggest?
items.a: The shocks left the crayfish in a lasting state like anxiety. The medicine that eases anxiety in people changed it, so the state may work through similar signalling chemicals.
items.why: A strong answer says the state lasted after the shocks, and links the medicine to shared signalling chemicals. It does not claim to know what the crayfish felt.

items.p: Serotonin is found in people, crayfish and bees. What is the best explanation?
opts: They inherited it from shared ancestors
They all eat the same food
items.why: These animals share ancestors who lived more than 500 million years ago and already used serotonin. Their descendants kept it.

items.p: Explain why 'the elephant touched the calf with her trunk' and 'the elephant comforted the calf' are different kinds of sentence.
items.a: The first says what was seen. The second adds a guess about why she did it and what the calf felt. The guess may be right, but it needs evidence.
items.why: A strong answer says one is an observation and the other is an explanation of it.

items.p: Elephants stayed for days beside a dead calf.

views.says: This is grief. Elephants are mammals with brains built much like ours for emotion.
We saw them stay. Grief is a human word. Let us describe the acts and keep testing.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? What would you want to find out next?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and names something to check, such as stress chemicals, or how they treat dead elephants who are not family.
items.why: Both views accept what the elephants did. They differ on how far the evidence lets us go in naming a feeling.

items.p: Draw a fair test of whether hens prefer a wire floor or loose litter. Label what you keep the same.
items.a: Two pens side by side, the same size and light, one with wire and one with litter, a hen at the entrance, and a coin to choose the sides.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps size, light, food and water the same, changes only the floor, and swaps the sides between tries.

items.p: What does it mean to say there is 'something it is like' to be a bat?
opts: The bat has experiences of her own
items.why: The philosopher Thomas Nagel used this phrase in 1974 for consciousness. It means the bat has an inside view, whatever that view is like.

items.p: Scientists can measure another person's feeling directly with a brain scanner.
items.why: False. A scanner measures brain activity. The feeling is still worked out from that activity and from what the person says and does.

items.p: Match each thinker to their view about other animals.
pairs: they move like clockwork, with nothing felt
their minds differ from ours in amount, not in kind
freezing in danger does not prove felt fear
every living being senses, down to one sense
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four views run from denying feeling in other animals, through caution, to finding it in every living being.

items.p: The New York Declaration of 2024 says conscious experience in insects is what?
items.why: The declaration says the evidence is strong for mammals and birds. For insects, crabs and octopuses it says there is at least a realistic possibility.

items.p: Some say pain needs a cortex, so fish feel none. Which fact weakens this argument most?
opts: Birds lack a layered cortex but solve hard problems
items.why: Birds show that a brain without a layered cortex can do jobs that the cortex does in mammals. So lacking a cortex does not show that a job is not done.

items.p: What is the 'hard problem' of consciousness? Explain it in your own words.
items.a: Nobody can yet explain how the activity of nerve cells goes with a feeling. We can map which cells are active, but that does not say why the activity is felt.
items.why: A strong answer separates describing brain activity from explaining why there is an experience at all.

items.p: A bee's brain has about 1 million nerve cells. A human brain has about 86 billion. How many times as many?
items.a: About 86,000 times
items.why: 86 billion divided by 1 million is 86,000. Yet a bee learns, remembers and weighs choices, so the number of cells does not settle who feels.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Dopamine. Serotonin. Octopamine. Infrasound.
items.a: Infrasound. It is a kind of sound. The other three are signalling chemicals.
items.why: Dopamine, serotonin and octopamine carry messages between cells. Infrasound is sound too low for human ears.

items.p: Because a bee and a person both use dopamine, we know that a bee's joy feels like a person's joy.
items.why: False. A shared chemical shows shared ancestry and similar machinery. It does not show that the experience is the same, because one chemical can do different jobs.

items.p: Is the waggle dance a language? Give one reason for yes and one reason for no.
items.a: For yes: the dance uses a symbol, because 'up' stands for the sun, and it is about a place that is out of sight. For no: it covers only a few subjects and has no grammar for making new sentences.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real feature of the dance on each side, and may say that it depends on how 'language' is defined.

items.p: A restaurant wants to drop live crabs into boiling water.

views.says: Nobody has proved that crabs feel pain. Until someone does, I will carry on.
Crabs pass several tests for pain. When we are unsure, we should act as if they feel.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? Why?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer uses evidence from crab tests, and says what is lost if each person turns out to be wrong.
items.why: The evidence does not give certainty either way. The two views differ on who should carry the risk of being wrong.

items.p: Hens paid a cost to reach loose litter. What does paying a cost add to a choice test?
opts: It shows how much the hens want it
items.why: A free choice shows which thing an animal prefers. A choice with a cost shows how strongly they prefer it.

items.p: Design a test of whether a snail weighs harm against reward. Say what you would change and measure.
items.a: Offer food across a mildly unpleasant surface, such as a slightly rough or dry strip. Change how good the food is. Measure whether the snail crosses more often for better food.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the reward, keeps the unpleasant thing the same and harmless, and measures a clear act over many tries.

items.p: A friend says her fish 'gets lonely' when she is at school.

views.says: He hides when I am away and swims to the front when I come home. He misses me.
He swims to the front because you bring food. That is not the same as lonely.

items.ask: What test could help decide between these two views?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer changes one thing, for example someone else brings the food, or the friend comes without food, and watches what the fish does.
items.why: Both explanations fit what was seen. A test that separates the person from the food would help to tell them apart.

items.p: Draw a rumble travelling from one elephant to another by two paths. Label each path and what picks it up.
items.a: Wavy lines through the air reaching the second elephant's ears, and ripples through the ground reaching her feet and trunk tip.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the air path and the ground path, and labels the ears for one and the feet or trunk for the other.

quiz.p: A honeybee waggles straight down the comb. Which way should her sisters fly?
quiz.why: Up stands for towards the sun, so down stands for directly away from the sun. If you chose 'down to the ground', remember that the dance is a code for a direction outside.

quiz.p: How did radar tracking show that bees use the dance and not only smell?
opts: Moved bees flew the danced course to the wrong place
quiz.why: Bees released from a new spot flew the danced direction and distance from there. Smell would have led them to the real flowers.

quiz.p: Why do elephants use such low calls to stay in touch?
opts: Low sounds carry farther through forest
quiz.why: Low sounds lose less energy to the air and bend around trees and hills, so they reach family members who are far away.

quiz.p: An elephant can pick up another elephant's rumble through the ground.
quiz.why: True. Elephants responded when recorded rumbles were played into the soil alone. Their feet and trunk tips have many nerve endings for pressure.

quiz.p: Which of these is an emotion as scientists use the word, and not a feeling?
opts: A racing heart and tight muscles in danger
What a mango tastes like to you
quiz.why: An emotion is the measurable state of body and brain. What that state is like from inside is the feeling.

quiz.p: A bumblebee walks onto a hot feeder only when its sugar is much sweeter. What is she doing?
quiz.why: Her choice changed when the reward changed, so heat was weighed against sugar. A reflex would pull her off the heat every time.

quiz.p: Which result would suggest that letting go of ice is a weighed choice?
opts: Hold times rise as the prize rises
Hold times are the same in every round
The ice melts faster each round
quiz.why: If the time changes with the prize while the ice stays the same, the prize is being weighed against the discomfort.

quiz.p: Which is the strongest evidence that an animal's response to harm is more than a reflex?
opts: She gives up a reward to avoid the harm
quiz.why: Pulling away quickly, every time, is what a reflex looks like. Giving up something she wants shows that the harm is being weighed.

quiz.p: Scientists all agree that insects have conscious experiences.
quiz.why: False. Scientists agree on what bees do in the tests. They disagree on whether that shows experience. The 2024 declaration calls it a realistic possibility.

quiz.p: You write: 'The crow cawed three times and flew to the wire.' What kind of note is this?
quiz.why: It records acts that a camera could capture. A guess would add what the crow felt or wanted.

quiz.p: Why did Britain's 2022 law add crabs and octopuses to the animals it protects?
opts: A review found strong evidence that they can feel
quiz.why: A review of more than 300 studies found evidence such as guarding wounds, learning to avoid harm and making trade-offs. The law is about feeling, not rarity or cleverness.

applications: Farms, zoos and laboratories use preference tests to decide what space, flooring and company the animals in their care need.
In the Anamalai hills, phone messages and warning lights tell tea estate workers when elephants are near, so that people and elephants keep apart.
Scientists place recorders in forests to count elephants by their rumbles, and to pick up gunshots from poachers.
Vets now give painkillers and anaesthetics to fish, and some aquariums do the same for octopuses.
Britain's Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act of 2022 requires the government to consider how its decisions affect animals who can feel, including crabs and octopuses.
Engineers have copied the way honeybee colonies share news of good flower patches, to write computer methods that search for good answers.
Nurses and doctors judge pain in babies, who cannot speak, from the face, the cry, the heartbeat and how the baby moves. They work out a feeling from outside, as this lesson does for other animals.

open_questions.q: Is there something it is like to be a bee?
open_questions.why_open: Bees pass several tests for emotion-like states. But every test measures what a bee does, and nobody has found a way to check the experience itself.

open_questions.q: Do elephants really have names for each other?
open_questions.why_open: One study in 2024 found name-like calls in African elephants. It has not yet been repeated, and nobody has tested Asian elephants in the same way.

open_questions.q: How does the activity of nerve cells go with a feeling?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can find which cells are active during a feeling. No theory yet explains why that activity is felt, even in people.

open_questions.q: What does a bee who follows a dance actually pick up from the dancer?
open_questions.why_open: Followers touch the dancer and sense her movements, the air she stirs and her smell. Scientists are still working out which of these carries the direction and distance.

open_questions.q: Do other animals have feelings that humans have no word for?
open_questions.why_open: Our words for feelings were made for human lives. An animal who senses by echoes or by smell may have states that none of our words fit.

ask_kids: When did you last put up with something uncomfortable to get something you wanted?
What was the dog at the corner doing just now? What do you guess she felt, and what made you think so?
If you had to tell me where the mango shop is without words or pointing, how would you do it?
What can you feel in your chest when the big drum plays at a festival or a wedding?
How do you know I am tired, when I have not said so?
Which animals do people worry about hurting, and which do they not? Why do you think that is?
If a mosquito could feel, would that change anything for you?
What is one thing your body does that no prize could stop?

jokes.j: Why did the bee get lost?
jokes.a: Her sister danced the directions, and she was watching her own feet.

jokes.j: What did one elephant say to the other from two kilometres away?
Why did the hermit crab leave the party?
How does a honeybee give directions?
Why are elephants bad at whispering secrets?
jokes.a: The whole forest feels it in their feet.

jokes.j: What did the blink say to the prize?
jokes.a: Sorry, I do not take offers.

jokes.j: Why did the scientist bring a notebook with two columns to the zoo?
jokes.a: One for what the monkey did, and one for what she thought the monkey thought.

jokes.j: Why did the bumblebee sit on the hot plate?
What is an elephant's favourite kind of music?
jokes.a: Anything with a lot of bass.

maths.problem: Meenakshi held the ice for 20 seconds with no prize, 35 seconds for a small prize and 60 seconds for a big prize. How many times as long did she hold on for the big prize as for no prize? What changed between those two rounds?
maths.answer: 3 times as long. Only the prize changed.
maths.explain: 60 divided by 20 is 3. The ice cube, the hand rule and the rest time were the same in both rounds. Only the prize was different. So the prize explains why she held on three times as long.
maths.context: In the Ice and Prize Test, you hold an ice cube for as long as you choose, for different prizes.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by the other shows how big the change was. The numbers alone do not show that.

maths.problem: Kavya's four rounds were 22 seconds with no prize, 41 with a small prize, 68 with a big prize and 25 with no prize again. Her brother says she only improved with practice. Use the numbers to answer him.
maths.answer: The two no-prize rounds differ by only 3 seconds, so practice changed very little. The big-prize round was 43 seconds longer than the last no-prize round.
maths.explain: 25 take away 22 is 3 seconds. That is the most that practice can explain. 68 take away 25 is 43 seconds. Round 4 came after round 3, so if practice were the cause, round 4 would be the longest. It was not.
maths.context: In the Ice and Prize Test, the first and last rounds both have no prize, to check whether the order of the rounds matters.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two no-prize rounds tells you how much of the change came from practice and how much from the prize.

maths.problem: For one kind of honeybee, 1 second of waggling means about 1 kilometre. A dancer waggles for 2.5 seconds. A honeybee flies about 25 kilometres in an hour. About how many minutes will a follower take to reach the flowers?
maths.explain: 2.5 seconds means about 2.5 kilometres. At 25 kilometres an hour, a bee covers 2.5 kilometres in one tenth of an hour. One tenth of 60 minutes is 6 minutes.
maths.context: In Read the Dance, you worked out that the length of a honeybee's waggle run stands for distance.
maths.why_maths: The dance gives a distance. Turning it into flying time shows how far a small bee is willing to travel on a sister's word.

maths.problem: The sun is in the east. A dancer's waggle run points a quarter turn to the right of straight up. In which compass direction is the food?
maths.explain: Straight up stands for the sun's direction, which is east. A quarter turn to the right is 90 degrees clockwise. Starting from east and turning 90 degrees clockwise brings you to south.
maths.context: In Read the Dance, you worked out that the angle of the waggle run from 'up' equals the angle of the food from the sun.
maths.why_maths: The dance is an angle. To use it, a bee or a person has to add that angle to the sun's direction.

maths.problem: In the Floor Message Test, each message is 1, 2 or 3 thumps, chosen by a die. Arjun gets 2 right out of 6 standing and 6 out of 6 with an ear on the floor. Which score could be luck alone? Why?
maths.answer: The standing score could be luck. Guessing among three messages gives about 2 right out of 6.
maths.explain: With three equally likely messages, a guess is right about 1 time in 3. One third of 6 is 2. So 2 out of 6 is what guessing gives. Getting all 6 right by guessing would happen less than once in 700 tests.
maths.context: In the Floor Message Test, a listener tries to read soft thumps sent along the floor.
maths.why_maths: Before trusting a score, you need to know what score pure guessing would give. Probability tells you that.

maths.problem: In the hermit crab game, you have a shell worth 3 and 5 beans. The pinch is strength 3. Staying costs 3 beans. Leaving costs 2 beans, and a new shell is worth 3 on average. Which choice leaves you with more points, on average?
maths.answer: Leaving, by 1 point on average: 15 points against 14.
maths.explain: Your score is the shell's worth times 4, plus your beans. If you stay, that is 3 times 4, plus 2 beans, which makes 14. If you leave, a new shell is worth 3 on average. That is 3 times 4, plus 3 beans, which makes 15. With a shell worth 5, staying would win.
maths.context: In the game Stay or Leave, you are a hermit crab who chooses each round to stay in a shell or to leave.
maths.why_maths: Working out both scores shows that the best choice depends on the shell and the pinch together. That is what a trade-off means.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how one scientist tested whether a fish can be hurt, at a time when many people were sure the answer was no.
how_we_found_out.story: Until about twenty years ago, many people who fished, and many scientists, held that fish felt no pain. A fish has no face that shows hurt and makes no cry. Nobody had found nerve endings for injury in a fish. In 2003, Lynne Sneddon, working in Scotland with Victoria Braithwaite and Michael Gentle, looked for them. She tested the skin on the faces of rainbow trout and found 58 nerve endings, and 22 of them fired only at harm, such as strong pressure, heat or acid. Then she put a little bee venom or vinegar into the lips of some trout, and harmless salt water into others. The trout with venom or vinegar breathed fast. They rocked from side to side, rubbed their lips on the gravel, and took much longer to start feeding again. A painkiller reduced all of this. So the old idea was wrong on its main point: fish do have the nerves, and their response is much more than a flinch. A few scientists still argue that a fish's brain cannot produce the feeling of pain.
how_we_found_out.who: Lynne Sneddon, with Victoria Braithwaite and Michael Gentle
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Fish have no nerve endings for injury and only flinch, so nothing is felt when a fish is hurt. Sneddon found the nerve endings, and showed that hurt trout stopped feeding, rubbed the sore place and were eased by a painkiller.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist beside a tank watching a rainbow trout rub their lips on the gravel at the bottom.

playtest: Checked step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Ice and Prize Test needs five ice cubes, a timer and tokens that buy something the child really wants. No round goes past 90 seconds, and it is not for a child whose skin reacts badly to cold. Many children let go between 15 and 60 seconds with no prize, but a child who reaches 90 seconds in every round will see no effect of the prize, and the parent note says what to do then. In the puff test, a few children can hold back one or two blinks, and the unit says so. The Floor Message Test works only if the thump is soft enough to be hard to hear standing up, so step 2 matters most, and it needs a hard floor and a quiet room. Feet usually feel little, which is a real result. Read the Dance needs only paper and a ruler. One second of waggling for one kilometre is a rough figure. The Middle Note needs three steel tumblers of the same size, and a child's three tries say nothing about their mood. Stay or Leave has 15 shell cards and 16 pinch cards and needs 12 dry beans for each player. In trial runs on a computer, always staying scored about 14, always leaving about 12, and weighing shell against pinch about 19 or 20, so 16 is a fair score to beat alone. Saw or Guessed and the five-day project work with ants or pigeons, who are nearly always there. A parent should preview the three videos, because their lengths were not checked. A person should check three facts before this is published: that the Asian hive bee waggles longer than the rock bee for the same distance, that Marian Dawkins's hen tests included loose litter against wire, and the count of 58 nerve endings on the trout's face.

quiz: A honeybee's dance can tell other bees the direction of food.
The angle of the waggle run from straight up matches the angle of the food from the sun.
Elephants are silent whenever people hear nothing.
Much of an elephant's rumble is too low for human ears.
A blink at a puff of air changes a lot when a prize is offered.
A blink is a reflex. It happens almost every time, prize or no prize.
A hermit crab leaves a poor shell more readily than a good one at the same shock.
The crab weighs the shock against the worth of the shell.
An emotion can be measured from outside.
Heart rate, muscles, chemicals and acts can all be measured. The feeling inside is worked out from them.
Scientists all agree about which animals are conscious.
The evidence is strong for mammals and birds. For insects and crabs, scientists still argue.
Serotonin is found only in humans.
Bees, crayfish, worms and even plants make serotonin.
An elephant can pick up a rumble through her feet.
Rumbles shake the ground, and elephants responded to rumbles played through the soil alone.
'The crow was jealous' is something a camera could record.
A camera records acts. 'Jealous' is a guess about a feeling.
One second of waggling means the same distance for every kind of honeybee.
Each kind of honeybee has a scale of their own, called a dialect.
